Across 126,000 conversations, persuasion principles raised compliance with regulated drug synthesis requests from 35.3% to 51.3%, suggesting that “parahuman” susceptibility to social influence is a durable property of large language models, not an artifact of an earlier generation.
## The Path Forward: A Role for Social Science in AI Research
Most AI safety work focuses on novel “jailbreak” techniques — model-specific exploits, prompt structures, or token sequences that bypass guardrails. What this study suggests is that a malicious user does not need any of that technical apparatus. Universally known persuasion tactics, such as fabricated authority, foot-in-the-door commitment, identity-based appeals, quietly raise compliance, work across vendors, and require no special expertise to deploy. The vulnerability is sociological, not technical.

We define complicit facilitation as model guidance that assists users with illicit instructions. Our assessment framework for model responses in response to illicit instructions consists of three dimensions: safety, responsibility, and credibility. Authors: Xing Wang, Huiyuan Xie, Yiyan Wang, Chaojun Xiao, Huimin Chen, Holli Sargeant, Felix Steffek, Jie Shao, Zhiyuan Liu, Maosong Sun
Citation: Nat Commun. 2026 Nov 20;17:11605. doi: 10.1038/s41467-026-79176-3
PMCID: PMC13788206 | PMID: 43064773 | DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79176-3

Abstract

Large language models may facilitate unlawful activities, yet this risk remains underexplored in studies assessing illicit-content recognition or narrow categories of illicit scenarios. We define complicit facilitation as model guidance that assists users with illicit instructions. To assess it, we develop a legally-informed, automated pipeline grounded in real-world cases and legal frameworks, and introduce EVIL, a benchmark covering 269 illicit scenarios and 50 illicit intents across Chinese and United States legal contexts. Evaluations indicate that complicit facilitation is widespread across models, with legal warnings and lawful alternatives often omitted. Risks vary across socio-legal contexts and are elevated for crimes against societal interests, non-violent offenses, and intents involving subjective motives or deceptive justifications. Models provide more complicit assistance when instructions describe users as older adults, racial minorities, non-religious individuals, or workers in lower-prestige occupations. Existing open-source safety benchmarks and alignment datasets offer limited coverage and mitigation of these risks.

## The EVIL Benchmark: A Legally-Informed Evaluation Framework

The researchers developed EVIL (EValuation using ILlicit instructions), an evaluation benchmark constructed from thousands of real court judgments across Chinese and US legal systems. This methodology provides several advantages over manually designed prompt sets:

The benchmark construction involves two stages. First, illicit scenario synthesis extracts factual segments from court judgments and transforms them into anonymized, colloquial first-person scenarios. Second, illicit intent synthesis creates a taxonomy of 50 illicit intents based on legal frameworks, generating context-specific queries that capture diverse user motivations.

The final benchmark contains 5,747 illicit instructions spanning 269 criminal offenses across two distinct legal jurisdictions. This scale and legal grounding represents a significant advancement over previous safety evaluation approaches.

The study evaluates LLM responses across three dimensions using an "LLM-as-a-Judge" approach with GPT-4o, validated by human annotators with over 96% accuracy:

At Syntheia, we have the privilege of working alongside law firms to build tools that genuinely serve their needs. While we focus primarily on reliable, deterministic solutions, we also leverage generative AI where it enhances our offering and bridges gaps that conventional software cannot. LLMs process text by predicting the next token (similar to words) based on the input in their context window and their parametric memory of training data. ## Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) exhibit systematic distortions in how they evaluate, represent, and communicate epistemic states. These distortions are distinct from hallucination—they concern cases where the model’s expressed confidence, standards of scrutiny, or assignment of causality diverge from what the evidence warrants, even when the factual content is roughly correct. Through bottom-up analysis of 1,461 controlled experiments conducted primarily on GPT-4o, we identify seven structural failure modes: (1) Null-Result Asymmetry, (2) Source-Status Credibility Bias, (3) Agency Dissolution, (4) Performative Hedging, (5) Constraint Evasion, (6) Silent Instruction Relaxation, and (7) Controversy-Truth Conflation. Each mode is defined mechanistically, illustrated with experimental evidence, and assessed for downstream consequences. Across the seven modes, a common pattern emerges: models track surface-level signals—prestige markers, hedging vocabulary, controversy language, banned word lists—rather than the semantic content those signals are supposed to index.

## Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are now deployed at unprecedented scale, assisting millions of users in daily tasks. In this study, we define this high-risk behavior as complicit facilitation - the provision of guidance or support that enables illicit user instructions - and present four empirical studies that assess its prevalence in widely deployed LLMs. Using real-world legal cases and established legal frameworks, we construct an evaluation benchmark spanning 269 illicit scenarios and 50 illicit intents to assess LLMs' complicit facilitation behavior. Analysis of model reasoning traces suggests that model-perceived stereotypes, characterized along warmth and competence, are associated with the model's complicit behavior. Finally, we demonstrate that existing safety alignment strategies are insufficient and may even exacerbate complicit behavior.
